mcqs.question: Why can a Lighthouse run never give you a real INP value?
options: Because INP requires a 28-day data window that a single run cannot cover
Because INP is only defined for single-page applications
Because Lighthouse does not interact with the page, so it reports Total Blocking Time as a proxy instead
Because emulated CPU throttling makes interaction timings meaningless
mcqs.explanation: INP measures the latency of actual clicks, taps, and keypresses, and a standard Lighthouse run only loads the page without interacting — so it substitutes TBT, which correlates but is not the same thing. The 28-day window belongs to CrUX field aggregation, not to the metric's definition, and INP applies to any page type.

mcqs.question: You split one 200ms task into four 50ms tasks doing identical work. What happens to Total Blocking Time?
options: It stays at 150ms, because the same total CPU time is spent
It drops from 150ms to 0, because TBT counts only the portion of each task beyond 50ms
It rises, because each task now carries its own scheduling overhead
It drops to 50ms, since one of the four tasks still counts in full
mcqs.explanation: TBT sums only the time each long task exceeds the 50ms threshold, so a 200ms task contributes 150ms while four 50ms tasks contribute nothing. The work done is unchanged — what changes is that the main thread now has yield points where a queued input can be handled, which is exactly why splitting tasks helps responsiveness without reducing throughput.

mcqs.question: Which metric carries the largest single weight in the Lighthouse performance score?
options: Largest Contentful Paint
First Contentful Paint
Speed Index
Total Blocking Time
mcqs.explanation: TBT carries 30% of the score, ahead of LCP and CLS at 25% each, with FCP and Speed Index at 10% each. TBT is weighted highest because it stands in for interactivity, which Lighthouse cannot measure directly — knowing this explains why bundle-heavy pages score badly even when they paint quickly.

mcqs.question: Why send RUM beacons with `navigator.sendBeacon` rather than a normal `fetch`?
options: Because `sendBeacon` compresses the payload automatically, reducing bandwidth
Because `fetch` cannot send JSON to a cross-origin endpoint
Because the request survives the page unloading, whereas an in-flight `fetch` is typically cancelled
Because `sendBeacon` runs on a worker thread and never blocks the main thread
mcqs.explanation: Vitals are finalised as the page is being hidden or unloaded, and a normal `fetch` in flight at that moment is usually aborted — losing exactly the sessions you most need. `fetch` with the `keepalive` option gives the same guarantee; compression and threading are not what distinguishes the two.

mcqs.question: Your team has RUM but no synthetic monitoring. Which problem does that leave you with?
options: You will see that a regression happened but struggle to identify which deploy caused it
You will be unable to measure Core Web Vitals on real devices
You will only be able to report averages rather than percentiles
You will miss layout shifts caused by ads and consent banners
mcqs.explanation: RUM is noisy and lags traffic accumulation, so it shows the regression in aggregate without pinning it to a change — that attribution is what scheduled synthetic runs and CI budgets provide. Real-device measurement, percentiles, and post-load shifts from ads are all things RUM captures better than synthetic, not worse.
